quiz.why: A stable patient gets the least invasive effective step first, and vagal maneuvers convert a meaningful share of reentrant SVT. Cardioversion is for instability, adenosine starts at 6 mg, and amiodarone is not the drug for narrow regular SVT.

quiz.q: A patient in monomorphic VT at 180 has a systolic of 72 and is confused. What is the correct treatment?
choices: Synchronized cardioversion at 100 J
Unsynchronized defibrillation at 200 J
Adenosine 6 mg rapid push
Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes
quiz.why: Unstable wide and regular VT with a pulse is synchronized at 100 J. Unsynchronized shock risks landing on a T wave in a perfusing rhythm, and adenosine or an infusion delays definitive treatment in an unstable patient.

quiz.q: You press sync and charge, but the defibrillator will not discharge on a wide irregular tachycardia. What is happening and what should you do?
choices: The pads are faulty; replace them
The machine cannot find consistent R waves in a polymorphic rhythm — switch to unsynchronized and defibrillate
The energy is set too low; increase it and retry in sync
The patient has converted already
quiz.why: Synchronization requires identifiable R waves, which polymorphic VT does not provide, so the device withholds the shock. Replacing pads or raising the energy does not create the R waves the sync circuit needs.

quiz.q: Torsades de pointes with a pulse is identified. What is the specific drug treatment?
choices: Amiodarone 300 mg
Adenosine 12 mg
Magnesium sulfate 1 to 2 g IV
Procainamide 17 mg/kg
quiz.why: Magnesium is the specific therapy for torsades. Amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT interval and can worsen it, and adenosine has no role in a polymorphic ventricular rhythm.

quiz.q: Three minutes after ROSC the patient's saturation is 100% on maximal oxygen and the blood pressure is 88/52. Which two actions are correct?
choices: Increase the ventilation rate and give a fluid bolus
Titrate the oxygen down toward 92 to 98% and treat the hypotension with fluid or a vasopressor
Maintain 100% oxygen and observe the pressure
Begin cooling and recheck both in 20 minutes
quiz.why: Hyperoxia injures reperfused brain tissue and post-arrest hypotension independently worsens outcome, so both are corrected immediately. Hyperventilation reduces cerebral blood flow, and cooling never precedes hemodynamic stabilization.

quiz.q: A patient achieves ROSC after a witnessed arrest. The 12-lead shows an inferior STEMI but the patient is comatose. What is the disposition?
choices: The catheterization laboratory, regardless of mental status
ICU only, because the patient cannot consent
Repeat the ECG in an hour before deciding
CT head first, then reassess
quiz.why: A STEMI after arrest goes to the cath lab whether or not the patient is awake, because opening the artery addresses the cause. Delay for repeat ECG or imaging forfeits myocardium, and coma is not a contraindication.

quiz.q: What temperature range and duration define targeted temperature management after arrest?
choices: 30 to 32 C for 12 hours
36 to 38 C for 6 hours
32 to 37.5 C held constant for at least 24 hours
Cooling to 28 C until the patient wakes
quiz.why: A constant selected temperature between 32 and 37.5 C for at least 24 hours, followed by fever prevention, is current practice; the specific number matters less than controlling it. Deeper cooling has not shown benefit and carries harm.

quiz.q: The physician says "let's get some epi going." Nobody moves. What is the best response from a tech?
choices: Wait for the physician to name someone
Draw it up quietly without saying anything
Say aloud: "I'll get epinephrine 1 mg IV," then report when it is in with the time
Ask the recorder to note the order
quiz.why: An unassigned order is the classic cause of a drug given twice or not at all. Claiming it aloud and reporting completion closes the loop; silent action leaves the leader unsure whether it happened.

quiz.q: How often should the compressor be rotated, and when?
choices: Every 2 minutes, during the rhythm check, in under 5 seconds
Every 5 minutes, whenever convenient
Only when the compressor says they are tired
Every 30 seconds to keep everyone fresh
quiz.why: Quality measurably falls after about two minutes, and the rhythm check is a pause that already exists, so the swap costs nothing. Waiting for fatigue means the fall has already happened, and 30-second swaps add needless interruptions.

quiz.q: Which combination of findings most supports a decision to terminate resuscitation in an adult?
choices: Witnessed arrest with bystander CPR and an initial rhythm of VF
Unwitnessed arrest, asystole throughout, ETCO2 persistently under 10 after 20 minutes, no reversible cause identified
A single dose of epinephrine given and no ROSC after 6 minutes
Core temperature of 27 C after 30 minutes of CPR
quiz.why: Unwitnessed asystole with persistently low ETCO2 and no treatable cause carries a near-zero chance of meaningful survival. A shockable initial rhythm and bystander CPR argue for continuing, six minutes is far too early, and hypothermia mandates a much longer effort.

quiz.q: A patient with an implanted defibrillator needs external pads. What is required?
choices: Place a pad directly over the device to shorten the path
Withhold defibrillation entirely
Position the pads at least 8 cm away from the device
Deactivate the device with a magnet first
quiz.why: Pads over the device can damage it and shunt current away from the heart, so at least 8 cm of clearance is maintained. External defibrillation is not withheld, and magnet placement is not required before an emergency shock.

quiz.q: How should the defibrillator be charged to minimize the perishock pause?
choices: Stop compressions, check rhythm, charge, then shock
Charge while compressions continue, then pause briefly to check rhythm and shock
Charge after the shock decision is documented
Charge only after everyone has stepped back
quiz.why: Charging during compressions collapses the pause to a few seconds. Charging after stopping adds five to ten seconds of no flow, and no step requires the team to be clear before the device charges.

quiz.q: An IO needle is placed in a patient's proximal humerus. Which statement is correct?
choices: Only crystalloid may be infused through an IO
Anything that can be given IV can be given IO, and fluids need a pressure bag
The IO must be removed within 15 minutes
Blood products cannot be given through an IO
quiz.why: The marrow drains into the central circulation, so drugs, fluids and blood all run through it, but marrow resistance means gravity alone will not deliver fluid. IO catheters remain usable for roughly 24 hours.

quiz.q: Which site should be avoided for an IO?
choices: A proximal tibia in a patient with a fractured left forearm
A proximal humerus in a patient with a tibial fracture
A tibia in which an IO was placed 36 hours ago
A distal tibia in a 70 kg adult
quiz.why: A bone used for an IO within 48 hours leaks infusate through the prior hole. The other three are acceptable sites — a fracture in a different limb, an intact humerus, and a standard distal tibia all pose no problem. Note that a fracture in the target bone, or proximal to the site in the same limb, would also be a contraindication.

quiz.q: An 18 kg child in pulseless VT has already received one shock. What is the energy for the second?
quiz.why: The second pediatric shock is 4 J/kg: 4 x 18 = 36 J. 18 J would be 1 J/kg, 72 J is 4 J/kg doubled, and 200 J is an adult energy.

quiz.q: A 2-month-old has a narrow complex tachycardia at 280 with no visible P waves and is mottled and poorly perfused. What is the correct intervention?
choices: Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg
Ice to the face and reassess in 5 minutes
Synchronized cardioversion at 0.5 to 1 J/kg
Fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg only
quiz.why: A poorly perfused infant in SVT is unstable and gets synchronized cardioversion at 0.5 to 1 J/kg, escalating to 2 J/kg. Adenosine and vagal maneuvers are for the stable patient, and fluid alone does not break a reentry circuit.

quiz.q: A 12 kg toddler in cardiac arrest needs epinephrine. What dose and volume from a 0.1 mg/mL syringe?
choices: 1.2 mg, 12 mL
1 mg, 10 mL
quiz.why: 0.01 mg/kg x 12 kg = 0.12 mg, and at 0.1 mg/mL that is 1.2 mL. The 1 mg adult dose is roughly eight times too much for this child, and 0.012 mg is a tenfold underdose.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old with severe asthma is now drowsy with a respiratory rate falling from 44 to 16 and a heart rate of 58. What does this represent?
choices: Improvement as the bronchospasm resolves
Compensated shock
Respiratory failure progressing toward arrest
A vagal response to the nebulizer
quiz.why: A falling respiratory rate with decreasing responsiveness and bradycardia is exhaustion and hypoxia, not improvement. In children bradycardia means hypoxia until proven otherwise and demands immediate assisted ventilation.

quiz.q: A newborn has been dried and stimulated. At 45 seconds the heart rate is 72 and breathing is gasping. What is the next step?
choices: Start chest compressions at 3:1
Give epinephrine via umbilical vein
Continue stimulation and reassess at 2 minutes
Begin positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 per minute
quiz.why: Gasping or a heart rate under 100 triggers positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute. Compressions wait for a rate under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation, and epinephrine comes later still.

quiz.q: Which statement about the pediatric assessment triangle is correct?
choices: It requires vital signs and a full set of numbers
It is a from-the-doorway impression of appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin
It replaces the primary survey
It applies only to children under 1 year
quiz.why: The triangle is a rapid visual impression that decides how sick a child is before anything is touched. It precedes rather than replaces the hands-on survey, needs no equipment, and applies across pediatric ages.

quiz.q: During a code the leader asks for the H's and T's to be considered. The patient has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on the right, and very high resistance when bagged. What should be prepared?
choices: Needle or finger decompression equipment
A pericardiocentesis tray
Calcium chloride and bicarbonate
Two units of blood
quiz.why: Unilateral absent breath sounds with high bagging resistance and distended neck veins is tension pneumothorax. Tamponade would give distended veins with bilateral breath sounds, and the metabolic and hemorrhage causes produce neither finding.

quiz.q: Which action most directly improves survival in a witnessed VF arrest?
choices: Early advanced airway placement
Earlier and more frequent epinephrine
Minimizing interruptions and shocking as early as possible
Obtaining central venous access
quiz.why: Compression continuity and time to defibrillation are the two interventions with the strongest survival evidence in shockable arrest. Airway, drugs and central access have never been shown to improve neurologically intact survival to the same degree.

quiz.q: A family member asks to stay in the room during a resuscitation. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Refuse; family presence is not permitted during resuscitation
Allow it only if the patient regains a pulse
Allow it if a staff member can be assigned solely to stay with them and explain what is happening
Allow it and let them stand wherever there is room
quiz.why: Family presence is supported by the guidelines and improves bereavement outcomes, but only when a dedicated support person is available. Unsupported presence distracts the team and harms the family.

scenarios.title: Adult VF arrest: two cycles to ROSC
scenarios.intro: `14:07`. A `58-year-old` man collapses in the waiting room and is brought into Resus 1 on a stretcher. He is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no palpable pulse. You are the first tech in the room. The physician arrives ten seconds behind you and takes the leader role. A second tech is at the door.

steps.prompt:
The patient is on the stretcher, still clothed, monitor not connected. The leader says, "Start compressions."

**What do you do first, and in what order?**

choices.text: Start compressions immediately, and direct the second tech to get the backboard under him and place pads on bare, dry skin
choices.feedback: Correct. Compressions start now; everything else happens around them. Naming the second tech's task out loud means the backboard and pads happen in parallel rather than waiting for the leader to assign them.

choices.text: Place the backboard and pads first so the rhythm can be seen, then start compressions
choices.feedback: This delays perfusion for 20 to 30 seconds at the moment it matters most. The board and pads can be placed during compressions with a brief lift; the rhythm will still be there in two minutes.

choices.text: Start compressions and wait for the leader to assign the pads
choices.feedback: Compressions are right, but the pads are the clock on this patient's survival. Anticipating and delegating them is exactly what an experienced tech adds to the room.

choices.text: Check for a pulse again to be certain before starting
choices.feedback: The pulse check is already done and the ceiling is 10 seconds. Repeating it because you want certainty costs perfusion — uncertainty is itself the instruction to compress.

steps.prompt:
Pads are on. The monitor shows a coarse, chaotic waveform with no organized complexes. Compressions have been running about `90 seconds`. The defibrillator is a biphasic unit; the manufacturer's label reads `120 to 200 J`.

**What is the plan for the next 30 seconds?**

choices.text: Charge to 200 J while compressions continue, then pause at the two-minute mark, confirm the rhythm, clear and shock
choices.feedback: Correct. Charging during compressions collapses the perishock pause to a few seconds. Confirm the rhythm in the pause, run the clear sequence including oxygen, shock, and hands straight back on.

choices.text: Stop compressions now, confirm VF, charge, then shock
choices.feedback: Same shock, worse pause. Charging takes several seconds, and doing it with hands off the chest is the most common avoidable interruption in a code. Charge first, then pause.

choices.text: Continue compressions for the full 2 minutes and shock at the next rhythm check without pre-charging
choices.feedback: The two-minute discipline is right, but not pre-charging adds five to ten seconds of no flow at the worst moment. The whole point is to have the energy ready when the pause starts.

choices.text: Deliver a precordial thump first, then charge
choices.feedback: A precordial thump has essentially no role in a monitored VF arrest with a defibrillator at the bedside, and it delays the one intervention that works. Charge and shock.

steps.prompt:
Shock delivered at `14:09`. You called "I'm clear, you're clear, oxygen clear, everybody clear," looked, and pressed. The monitor shows a brief flat period then chaotic activity again.

**What happens immediately after the shock?**

choices.text: Hands back on the chest for 2 minutes of compressions, no pulse check
choices.feedback: Correct. A just-converted heart is stunned and not ejecting, so a pulse check finds nothing and costs perfusion. Two minutes of compressions, then the rhythm check.

choices.text: Check a carotid pulse to see whether the shock worked
choices.feedback: This is the single most common post-shock error. Even a successful shock produces no palpable pulse for a while, so the check almost always reads as failure and always costs compressions.

choices.text: Reanalyze the rhythm first, then resume compressions
choices.feedback: You already know the rhythm; you just shocked it. Reanalysis belongs at the end of the two-minute cycle, not five seconds after the shock.

choices.text: Resume compressions and call out the time of the shock for the recorder
choices.feedback: Correct, and the time stamp helps the epinephrine and shock intervals stay honest. The essential half is that hands go straight back on the chest.

steps.prompt:
`14:11`. Second rhythm check: still VF. Second shock delivered. IV access is in. An i-gel is placed and waveform capnography connected; `ETCO2` reads `9 mmHg`. You have been compressing for four minutes.

**Two things need to happen. What are they?**

choices.text: Epinephrine 1 mg IV now, and switch to continuous compressions with a breath every 6 seconds
choices.feedback: Both correct, but incomplete. The ETCO2 of 9 is telling you the compressions are not generating flow — that number is an instruction, and it needs to be said out loud.

choices.text: Epinephrine 1 mg IV, continuous compressions with a breath every 6 seconds, and call out the low ETCO2 while swapping in a fresh compressor
choices.feedback: Correct on all counts. Epinephrine follows the second shock in a shockable rhythm. The advanced airway means continuous compressions at 10 breaths per minute. And ETCO2 under 10 means the compressions need to improve — after four minutes, that is you.

choices.text: Amiodarone 300 mg now, and keep bagging 30:2
choices.feedback: Wrong drug for this point and wrong ventilation. Amiodarone comes after the third shock for a refractory rhythm; epinephrine is due now. And with an airway in place, 30:2 discards the benefit of having placed it.

choices.text: Pull the i-gel — an ETCO2 of 9 means it is misplaced
choices.feedback: A sustained waveform at any value confirms the airway is ventilating. A misplaced airway gives no waveform at all. A low number means poor blood flow, and pulling a working airway makes everything worse.

steps.prompt:
`14:13`. Fresh compressor on. `ETCO2` has come up to `17`. Third rhythm check: still VF. Third shock delivered.

**What is the next drug?**

choices.text: A second epinephrine 1 mg now, since it has been 2 minutes
choices.feedback: The interval is 3 to 5 minutes, not 2, and the first dose went in at 14:11. More importantly, a rhythm that has survived three shocks is the indication for an antiarrhythmic.

choices.text: Amiodarone 300 mg IV push, with a second dose of 150 mg available if needed
choices.feedback: Correct. Shock-refractory VF after the third shock gets amiodarone 300 mg, followed by 150 mg if it persists. Lidocaine 1 to 1.5 mg/kg is the alternative if amiodarone is unavailable.

choices.text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg for the accumulating acidosis
choices.feedback: Bicarbonate is not routine in arrest. It is reserved for specific causes such as hyperkalemia or a tricyclic overdose, and giving it here treats a number nobody has measured.

choices.text: Atropine 1 mg
choices.feedback: Atropine has no role anywhere in the cardiac arrest algorithm. It belongs to symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse.

steps.prompt:
`14:15`. Mid-cycle, the `ETCO2` jumps from `18` to `44` and stays there. The compressor says the chest feels different.

**What do you do?**

choices.text: Say it out loud, stop at the end of the cycle for a rhythm and pulse check, and if there is a pulse start post-arrest care
choices.feedback: Correct. A sustained jump above 35 to 40 is ROSC until proven otherwise. Announce it, finish the cycle or check now per your leader, and confirm. Then oxygen down toward 92 to 98%, a 12-lead, a blood pressure, and pressors ready.

choices.text: Keep compressing and say nothing until the two-minute mark
choices.feedback: The number belongs to the whole team the moment it changes. Compressing on a perfusing heart for another 90 seconds risks inducing a new arrhythmia, and the leader needs this to decide.

choices.text: Stop compressions immediately and check a pulse
choices.feedback: Defensible, and many leaders will do exactly this. Say the number out loud first so the pause is a team decision rather than a compressor's unilateral stop.

choices.text: Assume it is a capnography artifact and continue
choices.feedback: A sustained rise of that size is not artifact. Dismissing it means continuing compressions on a beating heart and missing the window to start post-arrest care.

scenarios.debrief:
Eight minutes, three shocks, one round of epinephrine, one antiarrhythmic, ROSC. Almost none of the decisions that mattered were drug decisions.

The pattern is **protect the chest**. Compressions started before the monitor was connected, the defibrillator was charged while hands were still on, and the post-shock pulse check was refused. Every one of those choices bought seconds of flow, and flow is what defibrillation needs to have something to convert.

The second pattern is **capnography is a number you act on**. `9 mmHg` meant the compressions had degraded — which after four minutes was the compressor, not the patient. `44 mmHg` meant the heart had restarted, before anyone could feel it. Both were calls a tech makes out loud.

The third is **say things to a person**. "Get the pads" reaches nobody. "Leader, we are at two minutes" reaches the one person who needs it.

scenarios.title: Symptomatic bradycardia that needs pacing
scenarios.intro: `03:40`. A `74-year-old` woman is brought in by her son for two days of dizziness and one episode of passing out at the bathroom door. She is awake but slow to answer and says she feels "far away." Her son hands you a bag of medications. You are putting her on the monitor.

steps.prompt:
She is pale and diaphoretic. The monitor shows a regular rhythm at `34` with P waves that have no consistent relationship to the QRS complexes. Blood pressure cuff is cycling.

**What do you do in the first minute?**

choices.text: Get a 12-lead now, place pads pre-emptively, tell the physician the rate, pressure and that she is confused, and confirm IV access
choices.feedback: Correct. All four in the first minute. The 12-lead before anything changes the rhythm, pads on before they are needed, a factual report to the physician, and access because everything next needs it.

choices.text: Get the 12-lead and wait for the physician to ask for anything else
choices.feedback: The 12-lead is right and valuable. But a systolic of 76 with confusion is symptomatic bradycardia, and the pads, the access and the verbal report all save minutes you are about to need.

choices.text: Give oxygen at 15 L/min by non-rebreather and recheck in five minutes
choices.feedback: Oxygen is indicated only for hypoxemia, and 93% does not need a non-rebreather. Five minutes of watching a confused, hypotensive patient at a rate of 34 is five minutes lost.

choices.text: Ask the son for the full medication history before anything else
choices.feedback: The medication list matters enormously here and someone should get it — but not before pads, access and a report. Delegate it to the son or another staff member while you work.

steps.prompt:
The `12-lead` confirms complete heart block: P waves marching independently of a slow wide escape rhythm. The son's bag contains metoprolol and diltiazem. The physician orders atropine `1 mg` IV.

**What do you expect, and what do you set up while it is given?**

choices.text: Expect it to work and hold off on further setup until you see the response
choices.feedback: Atropine works by lifting the vagal brake on the sinus node. In complete heart block the failure is below the AV node, where the vagus has no influence, so a response is unlikely. Waiting to see costs three to five minutes.

choices.text: Expect little or no response in third-degree block; set up the pacer, draw up sedation, and make sure the pressor options are at hand
choices.feedback: Correct. Atropine is reasonable to try because it is fast and harmless, but it rarely works below the AV node. Setting up pacing and sedation in parallel is what makes the next step immediate instead of another five-minute delay.

choices.text: Question the order, since atropine is contraindicated in heart block
choices.feedback: It is not contraindicated — it is simply unlikely to work, and a single dose costs nothing while the pacer is being prepared. Raise unlikely-to-help as a preparation cue, not as a refusal.

choices.text: Prepare a second and third dose of atropine to reach 3 mg quickly
choices.feedback: The maximum is 3 mg, but grinding through it in a patient with high-grade block and a systolic of 74 spends the time that pacing needs. Escalate to pacing rather than repeat a drug that has no target here.

steps.prompt:
Atropine produced no change. Rate `32`, systolic `70`, and she is now harder to rouse. The physician says, "Pace her."

**How do you set it up?**

choices.text: Move to anterior-posterior pads, select pacer mode, set the rate at 70, and increase milliamps from low until every spike captures
choices.feedback: Correct. AP placement is preferred for pacing. A rate of 60 to 80 is the usual window, and current is increased from below until capture rather than started at maximum, which is needlessly painful.

choices.text: Leave the anterolateral defibrillation pads in place, select pacer mode, and start at maximum output to guarantee capture
choices.feedback: Anterolateral pads can pace, so that half is workable. Starting at maximum output is not — it is far more painful than necessary and tells you nothing about the threshold you will need to set output against.

choices.text: Select defibrillation mode and deliver 50 J synchronized
choices.feedback: Cardioversion treats a fast rhythm. This patient's problem is that the ventricle is not being told to beat often enough, which needs a pacer, not a shock.

choices.text: Set the pacer rate at 100 to maximize cardiac output
choices.feedback: Pacing at 100 shortens filling time and increases myocardial oxygen demand in a patient who is already poorly perfused. The window is 60 to 80.

steps.prompt:
At `70 mA` you see a pacer spike followed by a wide QRS on every beat. The monitor rate reads `70`. She groans and pulls at the pads.

**What are the two things that must happen now?**

choices.text: Confirm a femoral pulse at 70, and tell the physician she needs sedation and analgesia
choices.feedback: Correct. The QRS proves electrical capture; only a matching femoral pulse proves the muscle followed. And pacing is genuinely painful — her pulling at the pads is the reason, not a nuisance to be talked down.

choices.text: Confirm a carotid pulse at 70 and document capture
choices.feedback: Use the femoral. Pacer current makes chest and neck muscles twitch at exactly the paced rate, which feels convincingly like a carotid pulse and is not one.

choices.text: Increase the output further until she stops moving
choices.feedback: More current means more pain, not less movement for the right reason. The answer to a patient who is uncomfortable from pacing is sedation and analgesia, never turning it up until she tolerates it.

choices.text: Reduce the output to the minimum she tolerates
choices.feedback: Dropping below the capture threshold loses the only thing keeping her perfused. Set the output about 10% above threshold and treat the pain instead.

steps.prompt:
Femoral pulse confirmed at `70`. Output set to `78 mA`, about `10%` above threshold. She has received sedation and is settled. Systolic is now `96`.

**What happens next, and what is your job in it?**

choices.text: Cardiology consult for transvenous pacing, continuous monitoring, repeat vitals, and keep the pacer pads and settings untouched during transport
choices.feedback: Correct. Transcutaneous pacing is a bridge, not a destination. Your job is that nothing interrupts it: pads stay on, settings stay locked, the femoral pulse is rechecked after every move, and the transport monitor is ready.

choices.text: Turn off the pacer now that her pressure has improved and see whether she holds
choices.feedback: Her pressure improved because of the pacer. Turning it off returns her to a rate of 32 and a systolic in the 70s, and the underlying block has not been treated.

choices.text: Start an epinephrine infusion at 2 to 10 mcg/min and wean the pacing
choices.feedback: An infusion is a legitimate alternative or addition in symptomatic bradycardia, but weaning effective pacing in favour of a drug in complete heart block gives up a reliable mechanism for an unreliable one.

choices.text: Move her to a hallway bed to free the resuscitation room
choices.feedback: A patient dependent on transcutaneous pacing requires continuous monitoring and immediate access to the team. A hallway bed is not a place where a lost capture gets noticed in time.

scenarios.debrief:
The whole case turned on one piece of pattern recognition: **atropine treats the vagus, and the vagus does not reach below the AV node**. In complete heart block a dose is worth trying because it is fast and harmless, but the team that sets up the pacer during that dose saves five minutes over the team that waits to see.

The second pattern is **capture is a pulse, not a picture**. A spike-and-QRS on the screen looks like success and can accompany a patient who is not perfusing at all. Check the femoral, not the carotid, because the pacer makes the neck twitch at exactly the rate you want to believe you are feeling.

The third is that **pacing hurts**. A patient pulling at the pads is giving you information, not causing trouble. Sedation and analgesia are part of the procedure, not an afterthought.

And the medication bag mattered: metoprolol and diltiazem together explain a great deal about why an elderly heart slid into complete block. Always ask for the bag.

scenarios.title: Pediatric respiratory arrest
scenarios.intro: `19:20`. A father carries in a `3-year-old` boy, limp in his arms, shouting that the child stopped breathing in the car. He has been sick for three days with a cough and fever and stopped drinking today. You take the child straight to the pediatric resuscitation bay. Estimated weight from the tape has not been taken yet; he looks about `14 kg`.

steps.prompt:
From the doorway: he is limp, eyes half open and not tracking, with occasional gasping and blue lips. Nobody has touched him yet.

**What is your read, and what do you do first?**

choices.text: Respiratory failure. Open the airway and start bag-mask ventilation with oxygen immediately while someone attaches the monitor
choices.feedback: Correct. All three sides of the pediatric assessment triangle are abnormal: appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin. Gasping is not breathing. Ventilation is the treatment and it starts now, not after the monitor.

choices.text: Get a full set of vital signs and a temperature first so the picture is clear
choices.feedback: The doorway impression already told you he is in failure. A blue, limp, gasping child does not need numbers before he needs air; the numbers can be obtained while someone ventilates.

choices.text: Start chest compressions immediately
choices.feedback: Compressions come after you establish there is no pulse or a rate under 60 with poor perfusion despite ventilation. In a child the fix is almost always oxygen and ventilation first — jumping to compressions skips the treatment.

choices.text: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 L/min and lay the tape alongside him
choices.feedback: A gasping child moves almost no air, so a mask delivers oxygen to a face rather than to lungs. The tape is important but secondary. He needs positive-pressure ventilation.

steps.prompt:
You are bagging with a pediatric bag and an appropriately sized mask, two-person technique. The chest is rising. The monitor is on: heart rate `52`, and the pulse oximeter now reads `84%` and climbing.

**What does the heart rate of 52 mean?**

choices.text: A normal resting rate for a 3-year-old at night
choices.feedback: Not remotely. A 3-year-old's normal resting rate is roughly 80 to 120. A rate of 52 in a sick child is bradycardia, and in a child bradycardia means hypoxia until proven otherwise.

choices.text: Hypoxic bradycardia. Continue effective ventilation and reassess the rate and perfusion in about 30 seconds — if it stays under 60 with poor perfusion, start CPR
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the rule with no adult equivalent. Oxygenation and ventilation come first; if the rate is still under 60 with poor perfusion after that, compressions start even though there is a pulse.

choices.text: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg now for the bradycardia
choices.feedback: Atropine is for bradycardia caused by increased vagal tone or primary AV block, not for hypoxia. Giving it here treats the number and ignores the cause that is still killing him.

choices.text: Start CPR immediately since the rate is under 60
choices.feedback: Close, and defensible if perfusion is clearly terrible. But the rule is under 60 with poor perfusion despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation — you have only just started ventilating. Give it 30 seconds of effective breaths first.

steps.prompt:
Thirty seconds of effective ventilation later: heart rate `108`, saturation `96%`, and he has started making weak respiratory efforts of his own. Capillary refill is `3 seconds`, extremities cool.

**What has happened, and what comes next?**

choices.text: The bradycardia was hypoxic and ventilation fixed it. Keep supporting ventilation, get the tape weight, establish access, and check a glucose
choices.feedback: Correct, and it is the whole lesson of pediatric resuscitation: the rate followed the oxygen. He is not out of trouble — weak efforts still need support — but the trajectory reversed without a single drug.

choices.text: He is fixed. Stop ventilating and place him on a non-rebreather
choices.feedback: Weak respiratory efforts at a rate of 8 will not sustain him. Withdrawing support because the numbers improved is how a child slides back into failure while everyone watches the monitor.

choices.text: Give epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg since he was bradycardic a minute ago
choices.feedback: Epinephrine is for a rate under 60 with poor perfusion that persists after oxygenation and ventilation. His rate is 108. Treating the previous minute's number is a real and dangerous habit.

choices.text: Keep ventilating and get the tape, but defer access and glucose until he is more stable
choices.feedback: Ventilation and the tape are right. Deferring access and glucose is not — hypoglycemia is common in a child who has not eaten or drunk for a day, and it is quick to check and quick to fix.

steps.prompt:
The tape gives a weight of `14 kg`. Glucose is `58 mg/dL`. He remains cool peripherally with a refill of `3 seconds` and a rate of `132`. The physician wants a fluid bolus and dextrose.

**What volumes?**

choices.text: 280 mL of isotonic crystalloid as a bolus, and dextrose per protocol, then reassess perfusion
choices.feedback: Correct. 20 mL/kg x 14 kg = 280 mL. Reassessment between boluses is part of the order. The dextrose concentration and volume vary by protocol, but the hypoglycemia gets treated now, not later.

choices.text: 140 mL, a conservative 10 mL/kg, since he has a normal blood pressure
choices.feedback: A normal blood pressure in a child with cool extremities and a 3-second refill is compensated shock, not the absence of shock. The standard bolus is 20 mL/kg; 10 mL/kg is reserved for neonates and suspected cardiac dysfunction or DKA.

choices.text: 560 mL, front-loading two boluses so you do not fall behind
choices.feedback: Boluses are given one at a time with reassessment between, because a child with myocarditis or an overloading heart declares herself after the first. Front-loading removes the checkpoint that protects him.

choices.text: Hold fluids because his blood pressure is normal, and give dextrose only
choices.feedback: This is the classic pediatric trap. Children hold their blood pressure until they collapse, so a normal number with poor perfusion is the moment to give fluid, not the reason to withhold it.

steps.prompt:
After the bolus and dextrose he is pinker, refill is `2 seconds`, rate `118`, and he is breathing at `24` with mild retractions and a saturation of `98%` on a low-flow nasal cannula. He is starting to cry when touched.

**What is your job now?**

choices.text: Keep the bag-valve mask and airway equipment at the bedside, continuous monitoring, frequent reassessment of the triangle, and a warm blanket — he can deteriorate again
choices.feedback: Correct. A child who was in respiratory failure twenty minutes ago is not a stable child. The equipment stays, the monitor stays, and someone reassesses appearance, work of breathing and skin colour every few minutes.

choices.text: Break down the airway setup and return the pediatric cart
choices.feedback: Far too early. Children compensate and then fail abruptly, and rebuilding a setup mid-deterioration costs the minutes you saved the first time. Leave it until he leaves the department.

choices.text: Move him to a regular room to free the resuscitation bay
choices.feedback: He needs continuous monitoring and immediate access to the team until the admitting service takes him. Bay pressure is real, but this patient has not earned a lower level of observation yet.

choices.text: Document and let the father back in, then continue monitoring
choices.feedback: Reuniting him with his father is genuinely valuable — a calm child works less to breathe — and documenting matters. Make sure the airway equipment and continuous monitoring stay in place alongside it.

scenarios.debrief:
No shock, no epinephrine, no compressions, and the child recovered. That is what a pediatric resuscitation usually looks like when it goes well, because **children arrest from breathing, not from hearts**.

The number to carry out of this case is the one that did the work: a heart rate of **`52` in a hypoxic child**. In an adult that is a rhythm problem. In a child it is a symptom of hypoxia, and the treatment is air. The rate rose from `52` to `108` on ventilation alone, with no drug given.

The second pattern is **compensated shock hides behind a normal blood pressure**. Cool extremities and a three-second refill with a systolic of `88` is a child in shock who has not yet run out of compensation. Waiting for the pressure to fall means waiting for the last thing to go.

The third is that the doorway impression — the pediatric assessment triangle — was correct before anyone touched him, and every action that followed was set in motion by it. Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin, in about five seconds.
